item.title: Cloud Security Overview
item.description:
Cloud Security Overview

Cloud security is the protection of cloud-based systems, data, applications, identities, and workloads from threats and misuse.

Cloud providers operate large private networks, dedicated backbone connectivity, and high-scale infrastructure, but security must still be designed in layers. Organizations must protect not only the provider environment but also their own workloads, identities, applications, and data.

Core Security Areas

  • Physical infrastructure security
  • Virtualization and hypervisor security
  • Network security
  • Identity and access control
  • Data protection and encryption
  • Compliance and governance
  • Threat detection and response

item.title: Cloud Security Shared Responsibility Model
item.description:
Cloud Security Shared Responsibility Model

The cloud security model is shared between the cloud service provider and the customer.

The provider is responsible for securing the infrastructure beneath the customer workload, including physical facilities, network infrastructure, virtualization layers, and some core platform controls. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud, including identity and access, application security, data protection, configuration hygiene, and governance.

Examples of Shared Responsibilities

Layer Provider Responsibility Customer Responsibility
Physical security Data center security None
Network Core network and connectivity Security groups, routing, firewall configuration
Virtualization Hypervisor infrastructure VM hardening and workload protection
Operating system Managed platform services OS patching, access control
Application Platform services App logic and secure development
Data Storage platform protection Classification, encryption, retention
Identity & access IAM platform User provisioning, policies, least privilege

Security Controls

The model requires organizations to align identity, governance, configuration, monitoring, and auditing practices with the cloud provider’s model.

item.title: Facilities and Physical Security
item.description:
Facilities and Physical Security

Cloud providers must secure the physical locations where data centers operate. This includes protecting the facility itself, controlling access, and ensuring resilience against physical and environmental threats.

Key Controls

  • Secure location selection
  • Fencing and perimeter protection
  • Surveillance cameras and alarms
  • Mantraps and access control points
  • Guard patrols and building access procedures
  • Power redundancy and backup generation
  • HVAC, fire detection, and suppression systems
  • Safe handling of people, assets, and shipments

People Security

Security teams should apply strong hiring practices, background checks, separation of duties, role rotation, and strict employee termination procedures.

item.title: Hardware Security
item.description:
Hardware Security

The physical hardware that hosts applications and data must be secured by the cloud service provider.

Recommended Measures

  • Locked wiring closets and restricted access to MDF/IDF areas
  • No windows or secured windows only
  • Protected cable runs and communications infrastructure
  • Security cameras and intrusion detection systems
  • Hardened management stations
  • Strict control of access to data center floors
  • Biometric multi-factor authentication for authorized staff
  • Two-factor authentication at minimum for privileged access

Security Principle

Hardware security requires both physical barriers and administrative controls to reduce the risk of unauthorized access, tampering, and theft.

item.title: Virtualization Protection
item.description:
Virtualization Protection

Cloud providers virtualize resource pools and allocate them to multiple customers on shared hardware. This requires strong isolation and hardening.

Key Concepts

  • Hypervisor hardening
  • Patching and updating the hypervisor
  • Monitoring and logging hypervisor activity
  • Host OS patching
  • Instance isolation
  • Logical isolation and sandbox testing
  • Prevention of data leakage and inter-VM attacks

VM Escape / Guest Escape

A VM escape occurs when a process running inside a virtual machine interacts directly with the host OS or hypervisor.

item.title: Platform Security
item.description:
Platform Security

Platform security covers the controls used to protect the cloud platform and its services, including network protection, workload isolation, security policies, and continuous monitoring.

Security Controls

  • Firewalls and gateways
  • Proxies
  • Intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDS/IPS)
  • Honeypots and deception technologies
  • VPN and encryption
  • Authentication and authorization
  • Continuous improvement of platform protections

Network Security Considerations

Cloud providers generally have a vast private network and dedicated backbone connectivity. However, proper controls are still required to secure internal and external traffic paths.

item.title: Cloud Identity Introduction
item.description:
What is a Cloud Identity?

A cloud identity is any entity with access to cloud services or cloud resources.

Types of Cloud Identities

Human Identity

Examples include users, administrators, and developers.

Non-Human Identity

Examples include devices, software-defined infrastructure, AI workloads, and automated services.

Cloud Entitlements

An organization can grant both identity types specific cloud entitlements. Cloud entitlements determine which tasks an identity can perform and which cloud resources it can access.

item.title: Cloud Identity Challenges
item.description:
Cloud Identity Challenges

Cloud environments continue to grow, which makes it difficult for security teams to monitor and manage identities and their access privileges effectively.

Major Challenges

Lack of Visibility

Security teams often lose visibility of all identities active across the environment.

Inconsistent Security Mechanisms

Different cloud services often use different security policies and IAM capabilities, creating governance inconsistency.

Permissions Gap

Organizations frequently assign excessive permissions rather than following least privilege, creating unnecessary exposure.

item.title: Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM)
item.description:
Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM)

Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM) is a cloud security solution used to manage identities and cloud permissions according to the principle of least privilege (POLP).

CIEM uses machine learning and analytics to detect anomalies in account permissions within multi-cloud environments. This visibility allows organizations to apply consistent identity and access management across their cloud services and reduce the risk of data breaches and exfiltration.

item.title: CIEM Lifecycle
item.description:
CIEM Lifecycle

CIEM follows a continuous lifecycle that helps organizations manage identities and permissions securely over time.

Discovery

CIEM provides granular visibility into cloud identities and their entitlements by continuously analyzing cloud activity and policy structures.

This includes:

  • Human and non-human identities
  • Native and federated identities
  • IAM policies and resource policies
  • Access control lists and boundaries

Correlation

CIEM correlates permissions across cloud providers, because each provider uses different mechanisms and vocabulary for access control.

item.title: CIEM Protection and Remediation
item.description:
CIEM Protection and Remediation

CIEM helps organizations detect changes in privileges and respond before threats escalate.

Protection

  • Detect changes to entitlements and privileges
  • Identify privilege escalation and suspicious policy changes
  • Enforce entitlement guardrails
  • Support governance requirements such as CIS, GDPR, SOC 2, NIST, PCI DSS, and ISO

Detection

  • Monitor cloud resources and policies continuously
  • Detect suspicious activity and internal errors
  • Stream alerts to SIEM or UEBA systems based on policy

Remediation

  • Apply entitlement changes through cloud provider APIs
  • Route changes to ticketing or identity governance systems
  • Enforce changes in DevOps pipelines with Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

Purpose

CIEM ensures that identity and permission patterns remain aligned with policy and organizational risk tolerance.

item.title: CIEM Benefits
item.description:
CIEM Benefits

Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management delivers multiple operational and security advantages.

  • Granular cross-cloud visibility of entitlements from a single dashboard
  • Stronger overall security posture
  • Enforcement of least privilege
  • Reduction of unused permission risk
  • Monitoring, detection, and remediation of anomalies
  • Support for DevOps speed and agility without sacrificing security

Outcome

CIEM allows organizations to manage identity risk in a scalable and consistent way across multi-cloud environments.

item.title: Cloud Data Security
item.description:
Cloud Data Security

Cloud data security focuses on protecting confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data stored in the cloud.

Encryption and Data Sovereignty

Encryption is a core control for cloud data security and may be used to support requirements such as data sovereignty, compliance, and trust.

Key Management Models

  • Cloud provider-managed encryption
  • Customer-managed encryption keys
  • Customer-managed hardware security modules (HSM)
  • Bring-your-own-key (BYOK) models
  • Third-party encryption tools

Key Considerations

  • Internal data and sensitive data require stronger protection
  • Financial, HR, legal, and intellectual property data are especially critical
  • Trust, agility, and control expectations vary based on customer preferences

Security Objective

The goal is to ensure that data remains protected regardless of where it resides while allowing organizations to balance agility, governance, and trust.

item.title: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)
item.description:
Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)

Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) combines two main capabilities:

  • Security Service Edge, which provides network security as a service
  • WAN Edge, which provides network connectivity as a service

Core Elements

  • Secure Web Gateway (SWG)
  • Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)
  • Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)
  • Firewall as a Service (FWaaS)
  • Data loss prevention and TLS inspection
  • SD-WAN and WAN optimization
  • CDN and multi-cloud connectivity
  • Quality-of-service controls and SaaS acceleration

Design Goal

SASE modernizes network access by bringing networking and security together into a cloud-delivered architecture.

item.title: Secure Web Gateway
item.description:
Secure Web Gateway (SWG)

A secure web gateway is a security solution that prevents unsecured internet traffic from entering an organization’s internal network.

It helps protect users from malicious websites and supports regulatory compliance.

Core Functionality

  • URL filtering
  • Malicious code detection and filtering
  • Application control for popular SaaS services
  • Blocking access to malicious websites and links
  • Enforcing web use policies
  • Filtering traffic at the application level

Difference from Firewalls and Proxies

  • Firewalls inspect network-layer packets and compare them against known signatures.
  • Proxies filter outbound or inbound connections based on policy.
  • SWGs operate at the application layer and can evaluate web traffic more granularly.

Architecture Summary

SWGs sit between users and the internet, protecting good traffic while blocking malicious content and enforcing organizational policy.

item.title: Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)
item.description:
Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)

According to Gartner, a cloud access security broker is a security policy enforcement point placed between cloud service consumers and cloud service providers.

CASBs aggregate enterprise security policies and enforce them as cloud resources are accessed.

Common CASB Features

  • Authentication and single sign-on
  • Authorization and credential mapping
  • Device profiling
  • Encryption and tokenization
  • Logging and alerting
  • Malware detection and prevention
  • Data loss prevention and activity monitoring
  • Shadow IT detection

Scope

CASBs are mainly used to protect SaaS applications in the cloud. Their support for PaaS and IaaS is usually more limited.

item.title: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)
item.description:
Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)

Zero trust network access, also known as the software-defined perimeter, is a set of technologies and functionalities that enable secure access to internal applications for remote users.

Core Principle

Trust is never implicit. Access is granted on a need-to-know, least-privileged basis defined by granular policy.

Key Benefits

  • Remote users get seamless and secure access to private applications
  • Applications are not exposed directly to the internet
  • Network access is separated from application access
  • Risk from compromised devices is reduced
  • Access is limited to specific applications, not full network reachability
  • Lateral movement risk is reduced

Deployment Model

ZTNA uses user-to-application access patterns rather than traditional network-based trust assumptions. It often relies on end-to-end encrypted TLS micro-tunnels.

item.title: Native Cloud Security Controls
item.description:
Native Cloud Security Controls

Public cloud service providers offer a range of native security controls that help secure workloads, identities, networks, and applications.

Examples

AWS

  • IAM and SSO
  • Cognito
  • Security Hub
  • GuardDuty
  • Inspector
  • Config
  • CloudTrail
  • CloudWatch
  • Macie
  • KMS and HSM
  • Firewall, WAF, Shield
  • Certificate Manager
  • Secret Manager

Azure

  • Active Directory
  • Application Gateway
  • Defender
  • DDoS Protection
  • HSM and Key Vault
  • Front Door
  • Information Protection
  • Sentinel
  • Security Center

Purpose

These native controls help organizations secure their cloud operations with built-in provider capabilities and platform-native monitoring, identity, encryption, and compliance controls.
